title_content.content: Global Energy Storage: Have lithium prices peaked?

paragraph_content.content: Brian Ho, CFA
brian.ho@bernsteinsg.com
Neil Beveridge, Ph.D.

Kelvin Yuan, Ph.D., CFA

Lithium carbonate prices have tripled from 2025 lows, reaching ~$30k/t in May before easing to $20–25k/t on supply restarts, which we view as a short-term buffer. We continue to view the market as being in a mid-cycle recovery rather than approaching a peak. Inventories are tight at ~20 days, capex has yet to recover, and supply growth is starting to moderate. On the demand side, robust battery demand led by ESS continues to absorb higher prices. Taken together, we see further upside risks, with prices likely peaking closer to 2027.

Lithium demand has grown ~32% year to date, outpacing supply growth of ~24% and driving a meaningful market tightening. The key driver has been ESS, with demand up ~100% YTD, offsetting more moderate EV growth of ~9%. On the lithium supply side, growth has been led by China (+30%), Chile (+25%), and Argentina (+106%), while Australia (+6%) and Zimbabwe (+16%) have lagged, contributing to a tighter-than-expected balance.

We estimate ~200kt LCE of curtailed supply is gradually returning to the market although this only provides a short term buffer. While this may help partially close the supply gap in 2026, it is unlikely to keep pace with demand growth as capacity additions slow beyond 2026, leaving the market increasingly tight into 2027.

Inventories have tightened significantly, with lithium inventory days falling to ~20 days year to date. Historically, lithium prices tend to rise more sharply once inventory falls below ~20 days, with spikes often occurring closer to ~15 days or lower. Current levels suggest the market has moved from balanced toward tightening, with inventory now firmly within a range that has historically supported stronger pricing momentum.

Current higher lithium prices have not led to any meaningful demand slowdown. We expect ESS markets can absorb lithium carbonate prices in the ~$30k/t range based on underlying project economics. Importantly, sustained higher prices are required to incentivize new supply, particularly given long development timelines and the lag in capex following the recent downturn across the sector.

We have revised up our lithium price assumptions to reflect tighter lithium market. We now estimate lithium carbonate prices of ~$25k/t in 2026 (from $21k/t previously) and ~$32.5k/t in 2027 (from $25k/t), while maintaining our long-term price assumption of $16k/t. This reflects both tighter near-term market conditions and required to sustain long-term supply growth.

We expect the lithium market to remain a highly cyclical industry with supply responding elastically to price changes. Since our last lithium supply and demand update from last December (Global Energy Storage: 2026 Lithium Outlook. How high can prices go?), lithium carbonate prices have more than doubled and market sentiment has turned far more constructive. We still view the industry as mid-cycle rather than late-cycle. The key change has been stronger-than-expected battery demand, led by energy storage, which has tightened the market much faster than we previously expected. While lithium equities have already rebounded sharply, historical cycles suggest the move in the underlying commodity can still have room to run once inventories tighten and supply response lags. Lithium stocks often recover 6 to 12 months ahead of spot prices. In our view, the current rebound is consistent with the middle part of the cycle rather than the end, with the setup still supportive through 2027.

paragraph_content.content: Year to date, lithium demand has increased by around 32% while supply has grown by around 24%, implying demand has outpaced supply and the market has tightened materially. The key driver has been energy storage, with ESS demand up around 100% year to date compared with EV demand growth of around 9%. As a result, lithium inventory days have fallen to below 20 days, the lowest level since 2022, which has been a key driver of the sharp rise in lithium prices this year. Lithium prices remain highly correlated to inventory days. While the relationship is not perfect, prices have historically moved sharply higher when inventory falls below 20 days. With inventory now back in that range, the market appears to have shifted from a balanced market to a tightening market, which is more supportive for pricing than at the start of the year.

paragraph_content.content: The improvement in prices should lead to better profitability for lithium producers, but the industry is still recovering from a prolonged downturn. paragraph_content.content: The setup for 2026 is now more constructive than we had expected at the start of the year. We estimate full-year battery demand will grow by around 40%, translating into lithium demand growth of around 33% in 2026. In contrast, we expect new lithium capacity growth of only around 16% this year. This implies a further tightening in market balance, especially as demand is being pulled higher by ESS rather than just EVs.

In the long run, we still expect lithium demand to remain on a strong structural growth path, supported by EVs, ESS and wider electrification. However, the nearer-term point is that the market is tightening faster than the project pipeline can respond. Even if long-term capacity plans remain broadly intact, delayed investment over the last two years raises the risk of undersupply before the industry can scale again.

paragraph_content.content: Prices cannot rise indefinitely because end markets still need to absorb higher battery input costs. In our view, both the ESS and EV markets can still absorb lithium carbonate prices in the $30-35k/t range, especially given how sharply battery and system costs have fallen over the last two years. That suggests there is still upside room from current price levels of around $22k/t before demand elasticity becomes a more meaningful constraint. paragraph_content.content: Lithium supply remains relatively concentrated in Australia, Chile and China, but the growth mix this year has been more skewed toward China and South America. Processing capacity also remains heavily concentrated in China, which keeps China central to price formation and inventory trends. While China processes 80% of global lithium supply, China has a more scattered distribution of lithium mining projects, where the production split between brine and minerals is 40/60. More recently, China has accelerated the mining of low quality lepidolite to increase supply. Argentina is an emerging producer in the Lithium Triangle.

paragraph_content.content: Chile possesses the world's largest lithium reserves, primarily found in brines beneath salt flats like the Atacama Salt Flat. These brines have high concentrations of lithium, making them economically attractive for extraction. Lithium extraction in Chile primarily involves pumping lithium-rich brines to the surface and allowing them to evaporate, concentrating the lithium. The Chilean government has a target to double lithium output over the next decade with six new brine developments announced. The main companies operating in Chile's lithium industry are Sociedad Química y Minera de Chile (SQM) and Albemarle. Lithium extraction from brines can have environmental consequences, including water depletion in arid regions and impacts on fragile ecosystems. Chile's regulatory framework for lithium extraction has evolved over time, with the state playing a significant role in overseeing and managing lithium resources. There are ongoing discussions and considerations regarding the rights and involvement of indigenous communities in lithium mining projects. While Chile's extraction has focused on evaporation methods, the use of new DLE technologies is a core part of future development to reduce the country's use of water-wasting evaporation
ponds to produce lithium metal.

paragraph_content.content: The global lithium resource supply system is largely divided into two extraction methods: lithium extraction from ore and lithium extraction from salt lakes. Lithium extraction from hard rocks has increased faster than brine due to its mature and easy to scale industrial processes. Hard rock lithium deposits are found in several locations with most located in Australia, Canada, US, Brazil and Africa. Although lithium extraction from brine is lower costs, limited availability of high-quality brines and requirement of constant dry weather conditions are disadvantages. Lithium brine deposits are primarily found in the Lithium Triangle (Boliva, Chile and Argentina), US and China (Tibet and Qinghai).

paragraph_content.content: Taking a closer look at supply start-ups over the coming quarters, there is still a pipeline of projects that can add supply in 2026, alongside the return of around 200kt LCE of curtailed production. However, beyond the near-term ramp-ups the pace of new project additions still slows materially, which is why we think the market can tighten further in 2027.

Goulamina: Goulamina is one of the biggest lithium developments globally and started production of spodumene at the end of 2024. Stage 1 spodumene concentrate production is estimated at 506ktpa, increasing to a peak of 1MTPA in Stage 2. Ganfeng is the operator of the project after purchasing 40% stake on the project in May 2024. The Mali government has as 35% interests in the project with option to purchase additional 20% within first two years of operation.

Cuenca Centernario: Started production at the end of 2024. Operated by Eramet, the Centenario Phase 1 plant uses one of the most advanced DLE technology. Ramp-up is expected to be achieved by mid-2025. At full capacity, the Centenario Phase 1 plant will produce 24ktpa of battery-grade lithium carbonate. At full capacity, the cash cost for Phase 1 should be positioned in the first quartile of the industry cost curve (estimated at around $4,500 to $5,000/t-LCE). The drainable mineral resources amount to more than 15 Mt LCE, with an average concentration of 407 mg/L of lithium contained in the brine, supporting further capacity expansion.

Kathleen Valley: Liontown has commenced the production ramp-up of Kathleen Valley in 3Q24. In June 2022, the board of Liontown made the FID for the development of Kathleen Valley, clearing the way for the commencement of Project execution. The first spodumene concentrate has been produced following the progressive commissioning of the processing plant in July. Company targets a nameplate ore processing capacity of 3MTPA. The lithium producer said the concentrate produced thus far has a weighted average grade of 5.2% Li2O. Liontown has already committed 90% of its spodumene production for the first five years through offtakes with Tesla, LG Energy Solution and Ford.

Sal de Oro – Hombre Muerto: POSCO Argentina's project is divided into two phases. Phase 1 is located in the province of Salta and is close to producing lithium hydroxide. The first phase is for 25ktpa which completed test run in July 2024 and will be in full operation in mid-2025. Stage 2 is developed in the cooperation zone between Catamarca and Salta and focuses on the production of lithium carbonate.

Bougouni: KoThe Bougouni lithium project in southern Mali, operated by Kodal Minerals, is nearing completion and has achieved its first spodumene concentrate production in February 2025. Bougouni's stage one is to produce 125ktpa of spodumene from the Ngoualana pit. Stage two would produce 230ktpa from the Boumou and Sogola Baoulé deposits after $175 million in capital spending funded with stage-one cash flow.

Mt Holland: Covalent Lithium, a 50:50 joint venture partnership between Wesfarmers Limited and Sociedad Química y Minera de Chile's (SQM), has officially recognised the successful construction and commissioning of the Mt Holland lithium mine and concentrator in March 2024. Once construction of the Covalent refinery in Kwinana is complete and commissioned, Covalent Lithium will be a fully-integrated producer and supplier of premium, battery-grade lithium hydroxide for the global electric vehicle market. The project is expected to produce over 380,000 tonnes per year of spodumene concentrate.

Sal de Vida: In 2022, Arcadium Lithium commenced development of the 15,000 tonne per annum Sal de Vida Stage 1 project. The Sal de Vida deposit lies within the “lithium triangle”, an area encompassing Chile, Bolivia and Argentina that contains a significant portion of the world’s estimated lithium resources. The project is currently 66% complete with target for commercial completion in 2H26. The Project aims to produce 45,000 tpa in total from the planned staged expansions.

Mariana: The Mariana project is located in the Salar de Llullaillaco, in the province of Salta, Argentina. As disclosed recently in its 2023 Annual Report, Ganfeng Lithium said its Argentine Mariana lithium project produced the first batch of products at the end of 2024. Mariana is a lithium-potassium salt lake located in the Salar de Llullaillaco in Salta Province, and is run by Ganfeng's
owned subsidiary Litio Minera Argentina, carrying an investment of around US$600 million to produce 20,000 tonnes of lithium chloride or around 17,300 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent per year.

PPG: The PPG project consists of two lithium salt lake blocks, Pozuelos and Pastos Grands, with a total resource amounting to approximately 11.06 million tons of lithium carbonate equivalent (currently planning for a new round of resource survey). The project is located in the western part of Salta Province, at the center of multiple salt lake projects, possessing geographical conditions suitable for integrating surrounding salt lake projects into a large-scale mining operation. Currently, the planned annual production capacity of the PPG project is 50,000 tons of lithium carbonate, with salt field construction scheduled to commence at the end of 2023 and production expected to start in 2026.

paragraph_content.content: While 2025 was a challenging year for lithium producers, the setup for 2026 and 2027 looks constructive as market tighten. We estimate lithium demand to increase by 33% y-o-y rising from 1.7MTPA in 2025 to 2.3MTPA in 2026. Based on current planned capacity, average production capacity is expected to increase from 1.9MTPA in 2025 to 2.2MTPA in 2026 which is an increase of 16%. This implies that demand as a percent of average production capacity to increase from 88% to 102% implying further market tightening.

In the long run, we expect lithium demand to more than double from 1.7MTPA in 2025 to 4.4MTPA by 2030. To reach expected demand by 2030, lithium production capacity will need to rise to 5.2MTPA (assuming 85% utilization level). Based on cumulative capacity announcements, total capacity could increase from to 3.7MT in 2030. This implies a further 1.5MTPA of capacity additions from current planned levels through to 2030.

paragraph_content.content: How low can lithium prices go is determined by the price at which producers will start to cut production. Marginal cash costs provide a reliable floor for lithium prices. According to our analysis, the marginal cash cost of lithium at 90th percentile is around US\$11.1k/ton which will see supply cuts below this price. In 2020, the price of lithium remained close to marginal cost for 12 months, before rising rapidly. We are currently about a year below this cash costs level so it's aligned with previous cycle as higher cost producers have cut supply.

The full supply costs are higher than cash costs as it accounts for the capital costs of the project and depreciation over the life of the mine. Lithium price will trade above this level during market deficit or below with oversupply. We expect the long term price is US\$16k/ton based on our expectation of full supply costs for the industry. paragraph_content.content: On the flip side, how high can prices go is determined by the price at which buyers are less willing to buy lithium. In other words, at what price will we see demand destruction? At $100/kWh battery pack price or lower, OEMs can produce and sell EVs at $30k price level and compete with ICE vehicles in the mass market. For NMC batteries, this can be achieved at lithium carbonate price of $20k/t. Alternatively, for LFP batteries, lithium prices can go up to $40k/t level for EVs to compete with ICE. The conclusion is that lithium prices can stay above long term price as EVs remain affordable. Reaching historical high of $80k/t is almost certainly impossible.

That suggests there is still upside room from current price levels of around $25k/t before demand elasticity becomes a more meaningful constraint. Overall, lithium price movements have a meaningful but not dominant impact on full ESS system cost because lithium is a big driver of cell prices but cells are only one part of the installed system.

paragraph_content.content: Overall, we continue to believe lithium prices bottomed in 2025, but the market has since moved faster than expected and is now in a clear tightening phase. The industry still shows the classic features of a mid-cycle recovery: prices have rebounded, inventories have tightened, curtailed supply is starting to return, but new greenfield investment is still lagging. That combination should remain supportive through 2027.

paragraph_content.content: The improvement in prices should lead to better profitability for lithium producers, but the industry is still recovering from a prolonged downturn. Returns on capital have been compressed for the last two years and balance sheets remain a focus for management teams. This matters because even with a stronger price signal today, the supply side is unlikely to respond immediately given prior capex cuts and the time needed to restart or expand operations.

paragraph_content.content: Capex peaked at the end of 2023 and fell materially through 2024 and 2025 as producers focused on preserving balance sheets. Even though spot prices have recovered, the investment response should lag because managers are unlikely to reverse course immediately after a deep downturn. In our view, that lagged capex response is one of the main reasons the market can remain tight through 2026 and into 2027.

paragraph_content.content: Within our coverage, Tianqi Lithium is a top pick given our positive lithium price outlook. Tianqi is one of the largest pure-play lithium producer globally with the highest returns in the battery value chain. The company has a track record of delivering superior margins driven by lower costs and asset integration. By leveraging the high-quality and low-cost lithium concentrate from the Greenbushes Mine, Tianqi is able to achieve self-sufficiency in lithium raw materials for efficient manufacturing of high-quality lithium compounds and derivatives. We expect Tianqi's share price will continue to rise ahead of our higher lithium price outlook through 2026 and 2027. Tianqi's share price has historically moved 6-12 months ahead of spot lithium carbonate prices.

paragraph_content.content: Tianqi Lithium typically shows operating margins that rise and fall in tandem with lithium carbonate prices. When lithium carbonate prices were very high in 2022-23, Tianqi's operating exceeded 70% but as lithium prices collapsed through 2023–2024, margins compressed sharply and the company even reported periods of net loss despite still-positive operating margins. Even though the relationship is not perfectly linear due to hedging, product mix shifts, and evolving contract versus spot pricing, we expect margins have bottomed in 2025 and will increase over 2026 and 2027.
